intro: A quiet upward leap receives a forceful answer, and the finale builds an entire argument from that opposition. Follow the lyrical second idea into the recapitulation: it returns without rescuing the symphony from G minor.
question: Does the lyrical second idea sound changed when it returns in the home minor key?

sections.mNote: Quiet upward figure and forceful reply

cues.title: A leap and an answer
cues.text: The opening string figure climbs through the notes of a chord, then receives a much stronger answer. Keep that question-and-answer contrast in mind: the upward shape can be broken apart later without losing its identity.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf IV, bars 1–16, PDF pp. 33–34; report begins quietly at −24.4 dB and rises over the opening paragraph. No single answer is timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Running figures carry weight
cues.text: Listen below the top melody. Fast string figures pass through different registers while winds and horns give the more forceful statements their weight. The motion continues even when the main idea is briefly absent.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf IV, bars 30–60, PDF pp. 35–36; report boundary 0:28 and higher relative level from 0:30 to 0:55.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A more lyrical voice
cues.text: The second group offers a quieter, more sustained idea in B♭ major. The contrast is not a new tempo: the accompanying pulse still belongs to the same fast movement.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf IV, second group, PDF pp. 37–38; report’s strongest boundary is 1:06, with level falling to −25.3 dB at 1:05 and B♭-centred estimates at 1:10–1:25.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: No final commission known
cues.text: The intended occasion for Mozart’s last three symphonies remains uncertain. Their close dates in his catalogue do not prove that they were conceived as a farewell or that he knew they would be his last.
cues.evidence: Marianne Williams Tobias, Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra programme note, Symphony No. 40 (2015), https://www.indianapolissymphony.org/backstage/program-notes/mozart-symphony-no-40/. Composer biography, final-symphony context.

cues.title: The leap loses its footing
cues.text: In the development, the familiar upward gesture encounters chromatic notes and moving harmonic ground. Imitative exchanges let separate parts pursue the same fragment instead of presenting a new tune over a stable accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf IV, bars 125–170, PDF pp. 40–42; report boundaries 2:00 and 2:10 precede an active span with changing pitch regions at 2:15–2:45. Timing is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: No victory added
cues.text: This symphony has neither trumpets nor timpani. Its conclusion will use the same wind, horn and string resources, and the minor key is not exchanged for a ceremonial major-key ending.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf orchestral score and final G-minor cadence, PDF p. 49. This describes the written scoring and ending, not a newly detected instrument.

cues.title: Home does not mean calm
cues.text: The recapitulation brings the rising figure back to G minor. The music still has to revisit the second group; the return of the first theme is the start of another argument, not the end of one.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf IV, bars 206 onward, PDF p. 44; report boundary 3:08 and return of the opening pitch profile around 3:10–3:25. This cue describes the recapitulation passage, not its first bar.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A familiar line darkened
cues.text: The lyrical material now belongs to G minor. Listen for how a recognisable melodic shape changes character when its new tonal setting removes the earlier major-key contrast.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf IV, recapitulated second group, PDF pp. 46–47; report lower relative level at 3:45–3:55 and G-minor-centred windows through 4:00–4:10.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The source leaves a gap
cues.text: Musopen’s release makes this performance freely available, but it does not identify a conductor or a recording session. The release year is not used here as a substitute for the date the musicians played.
cues.evidence: Commons file page and upstream MusopenCollectionAsFlac metadata; session and conductor remain unknown in this recording’s dossier.

transitions.title: A forceful paragraph makes room
transitions.how: The transition concentrates its energy on the dominant of B♭. A reduction in texture then lets the quieter second group establish the relative major. The contrast comes from a new melodic manner and lighter accompaniment, not from a new basic tempo.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf IV, transition and second-group opening, PDF pp. 36–37; report strong boundary 1:06 and sharp relative-level fall at 1:05.

transitions.title: The opening gesture is destabilised
transitions.how: After the exposition’s B♭-major close, the upward gesture returns in a chromatically disrupted unison. The familiar contour is retained while its comfortable chordal basis is removed. Short fragments then become material for imitative, sequential working.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf IV, bars 118–140, PDF p. 40; report boundaries 2:00 and 2:10 mark the changed texture. The development marker at 1:56 is proportional, not an aligned attack.

transitions.title: The restless passage finds G
transitions.how: The development’s running fragments lead back to the dominant of G minor. The quiet opening gesture returns over its original tonic, followed by the forceful answer. The recognisable texture helps make the tonal return audible.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf IV, bars 193–214, PDF p. 44; report level falls around 3:05 and opening pitch material recurs after boundary 3:08.

transitions.title: The lyrical idea changes key
transitions.how: The return of the second group is prepared within the home-key argument rather than by another escape to B♭ major. Its quieter melody now settles in G minor. Mozart retains the textural contrast while removing the exposition’s contrast of tonal centres.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf IV, recapitulatory transition and second group, PDF pp. 45–47; report low-level windows at 3:45–3:55 and boundaries 3:48 and 3:52. Timing remains provisional.

source.title: Mozart, Symphony No. 40, K. 550, Breitkopf & Härtel, Mozarts Werke VIII/40 (1880), plate W.A.M. 550; parts common to both versions
source.locator: IV. Allegro assai; PDF pp. 33–49, especially bars 1–16, 44–60, 79–110, 125–140, 193–214 and 293–308. Both versions are printed together. Clarinets and version-specific oboe detail are not inferred from this recording. Timings are provisional passage estimates, not aligned entrances.

timeline.note: Opening passage: the quiet upward violin gesture is supported by the lower parts.
Transition passage: winds and horns reinforce running string figures.
Quieter second-group passage; strings and wind replies alternate rather than playing continuously.
Development: chromatic unison and subsequent imitation disrupt the opening gesture.
The quiet opening texture returns in the recapitulation.
The lyrical second group returns in G minor, with version-specific wind detail withheld.
Closing paragraph: running strings and sustained or punctuating wind-and-horn chords.

Salzburg · Italy · Mannheim and Paris · Vienna from 1781

composer.background:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the seventh child of Leopold Mozart and Anna Maria Pertl; only he and his sister Maria Anna survived infancy. Leopold was a violinist and composer in the archbishop’s service, and in the year of Wolfgang’s birth published an influential violin treatise. He taught both children. Maria Anna, called Nannerl within the family, became an accomplished keyboard player, and the first tours presented brother and sister together. The family’s travels were an educational system as well as a business: the children encountered instruments, performers, repertories and audiences that a Salzburg childhood alone could not have supplied.

The long tour of 1763–66 took them through German courts, Paris, London and the Netherlands. In London Mozart met Johann Christian Bach, whose clear phrases and Italianate melodic style offered a model different from the contrapuntal teaching associated with Bach’s father. Illness repeatedly interrupted the itinerary. Leopold managed engagements, publicity and money while supervising composition, and the surviving correspondence documents the costs and uncertainties behind the public demonstrations. Wolfgang learned to write for named performers and immediate occasions before he had an independent adult household.
composer.epithet: An opera composer whose instrumental music gives different voices the freedom to disagree.
